knowledge.summary: Compute, for every cell, the minimum number of edge-sharing moves needed to reach any cell containing 0.
knowledge.pattern: Multi-source breadth-first search on an unweighted grid. Treat every 0 cell as a source and expand from all sources simultaneously.
algorithm: Create an m x n distance matrix initialized to -1, where -1 means unvisited.
Add every cell containing 0 to a FIFO queue and set its distance to 0.
Repeatedly remove a cell from the front of the queue.
Inspect its four edge-sharing neighbors.
For each in-bounds neighbor whose distance is still -1, set its distance to the current cell's distance plus 1 and add it to the queue.
After the queue is empty, return the distance matrix.
pitfalls: Running a separate search from every 1 cell can be unnecessarily expensive.
The queue must initially contain all 0 cells, not just one of them.
Mark a neighbor as visited when it is enqueued, rather than when it is dequeued, to avoid duplicate work.
Only consider the four edge-sharing directions; diagonal movement is not allowed.
Check row and column bounds before accessing a neighbor.
Use a true FIFO queue or an index-based queue implementation; repeatedly removing the first element of an array may be costly in some languages.
knowledge.timeComplexity: O(m * n), because each cell is enqueued and processed at most once.
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(m * n) for the distance matrix and BFS queue.
knowledge.hint1: Think of the matrix as an unweighted graph where each cell is connected to its edge-sharing neighbors.
knowledge.hint2: Instead of searching outward from every 1, consider beginning the search from all cells that already have distance 0.
knowledge.hint3: Initialize one BFS queue with every 0 cell. The first time an unvisited cell is reached, its distance is one more than the distance of the cell that reached it.

knowledge.summary: Determine whether the final 0 is decoded as a standalone one-bit character. Since every 0 starts a one-bit character and every 1 starts a two-bit character, the decoding can be simulated deterministically from left to right.
knowledge.pattern: Greedy left-to-right traversal with variable step size.
algorithm: Initialize an index i to 0.
While i is before the last array position, advance by 1 if bits[i] is 0; otherwise, advance by 2.
After the traversal, return true if i equals the last index.
If i has moved past the last index, the final 0 was consumed as the second bit of a two-bit character, so return false.
pitfalls: Stop the loop before processing the last position; using i < n instead of i < n - 1 can produce the wrong conclusion.
A 1 always begins a two-bit character, so advance by exactly 2 when bits[i] is 1.
Do not decide based only on the final two bits; the decoding alignment depends on earlier bits.
knowledge.hint1: Process the bits from left to right and consider how the current bit determines the character length.
knowledge.hint2: At a 0, move forward one position; at a 1, move forward two positions.
knowledge.hint3: Stop before decoding the final array position. If your index lands exactly on that position, the answer is true.

knowledge.summary: Detect whether there are indices i < j < k such that nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]. Scan from right to left so the elements that could serve as nums[j] and nums[k] are already known when considering nums[i].
knowledge.pattern: Reverse traversal with a monotonic decreasing stack. The stack stores candidates for the larger value nums[j], while a separate variable stores the best confirmed candidate for the middle value nums[k].
algorithm: Initialize an empty stack and set middle to negative infinity.
Traverse nums from right to left, letting the current value be x.
If x < middle, return true: x can be nums[i], and the previously established pair provides nums[j] and nums[k].
While the stack is not empty and x > stack.top, pop the stack and assign the popped value to middle. Here x becomes a candidate for nums[j], and each popped value is a candidate for nums[k].
Push x onto the stack.
If the traversal finishes without finding x < middle, return false.
pitfalls: All inequalities are strict. Use x > stack.top when popping and x < middle when detecting the pattern.
Do not pop equal values, because nums[k] must be strictly smaller than nums[j].
Check x < middle before modifying middle using the current element; nums[i] must occur before the established nums[j] and nums[k].
Traverse from right to left. A left-to-right implementation does not preserve the same index-order invariant.
Initialize middle with a value smaller than every possible nums[i], such as negative infinity or an integer sentinel safely below the stated value range.
knowledge.timeComplexity: O(n), because each element is pushed onto and popped from the stack at most once.
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(n) in the worst case for the monotonic stack.
knowledge.hint1: Try scanning from right to left, where every previously processed element is guaranteed to have a larger index than the current element.
knowledge.hint2: Maintain a decreasing stack of possible values for the '3' in the 132 pattern.
knowledge.hint3: Whenever a larger current value pops smaller stack values, the last popped value becomes a confirmed candidate for the '2'. A later value smaller than that candidate completes the pattern.

knowledge.summary: Repeatedly choose two current values, combine them with one allowed binary operator, and recurse with the result replacing those two values. When only one value remains, check whether it is approximately 24.
knowledge.pattern: Backtracking over pairwise reductions. This explores operand order, operator choice, and all possible parenthesizations without explicitly generating expression strings.
algorithm: Convert the four card values to real numbers.
Define DFS on the current list of values.
If one value remains, return whether its distance from 24 is below a small epsilon.
Otherwise, choose every ordered pair of distinct indices i and j.
Create a new list containing all values except nums[i] and nums[j].
Try nums[i] + nums[j], nums[i] - nums[j], nums[i] * nums[j], and nums[i] / nums[j].
Skip division when nums[j] is approximately zero.
Append each result to the remaining list and recurse. Return true immediately if any branch succeeds.
If every pair and operation fails, return false.
pitfalls: Use real division rather than integer division.
Compare floating-point results with an epsilon instead of exact equality.
Never divide by zero or by a value sufficiently close to zero.
Subtraction and division are not commutative, so both operand orders must be explored.
Each card must be consumed exactly once; replacing two selected values with their result enforces this.
Do not introduce unary negation or concatenate card values.
If unordered pairs are used instead of ordered pairs, explicitly generate both a-b and b-a, and both valid division orders.
knowledge.timeComplexity: Because cards.length is fixed at 4, the search is O(1). Generalized to n values with ordered pairs and four operators, an upper bound is O(4^(n-1) * n! * (n-1)!), excluding list-copying costs.
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(1) for the fixed input size. Generalized to n values, recursion depth is O(n); constructing a new list at each level can use O(n^2) space along one recursion path.
knowledge.hint1: Think about evaluating an expression from the bottom up: one operation combines two available values into one new value.
knowledge.hint2: At each step, try choosing two current values and replacing them with the result of one allowed operation.
knowledge.hint3: Use DFS until one value remains. Explore ordered pairs so subtraction and division cover both directions, and use an epsilon when checking against 24 or zero.

knowledge.summary: Find every distinct value triplet whose elements come from three different indices and sum to zero. Sorting allows duplicate values to be handled systematically and turns the search for the remaining two values into a two-pointer scan.
algorithm: Sort nums in nondecreasing order.
Iterate i from 0 through n - 3, treating nums[i] as the first value.
If nums[i] is positive, stop because every subsequent value is at least nums[i], so no later triplet can sum to zero.
If i > 0 and nums[i] equals nums[i - 1], skip this iteration to avoid repeating triplets with the same first value.
Initialize left = i + 1 and right = n - 1.
While left < right, compute sum = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right].
If sum is less than zero, increment left to increase the sum.
If sum is greater than zero, decrement right to decrease the sum.
If sum equals zero, record the triplet, move both pointers inward, and skip values equal to the values just used on both sides.
Return all recorded triplets.
pitfalls: Do not use the same array index more than once; maintaining i < left < right guarantees distinct indices.
Skipping duplicate first values is necessary but insufficient; duplicates must also be skipped after finding a valid pair.
Only skip left and right duplicates after recording a valid triplet. Ordinary pointer movement for sums below or above zero is enough.
Always check left < right while skipping duplicates to avoid crossing the pointers or accessing outside the active range.
The early termination nums[i] > 0 is valid only because the array has been sorted.
Include the sorting cost when analyzing time and auxiliary space.
knowledge.timeComplexity: O(n^2): sorting costs O(n log n), and each fixed first element performs an O(n) two-pointer scan.
knowledge.spaceComplexity: Excluding the returned triplets, auxiliary space depends on the sorting implementation: commonly O(log n) for the sorting call stack, though some implementations may use O(n).
knowledge.hint1: Consider arranging the values so that equal elements are adjacent and moving toward larger or smaller sums becomes predictable.
knowledge.hint2: After fixing one value, the other two must sum to its negation. In a sorted array, try searching for that pair from opposite ends.
knowledge.hint3: Skip a repeated fixed value. After finding a triplet, move both pointers inward and skip repeated values at each pointer so the same value triplet is not emitted again.

knowledge.summary: Sort the array, fix one number, and use two pointers to find the pair whose total with the fixed number is closest to the target.
algorithm: Sort nums in nondecreasing order.
Initialize the closest sum to nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2].
For each index i from 0 to n - 3, set left = i + 1 and right = n - 1.
While left < right, compute sum = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right].
If |sum - target| is smaller than the current best difference, update the closest sum.
If sum equals target, return target immediately.
If sum is less than target, increment left to increase the sum; otherwise, decrement right to decrease it.
Return the closest sum after all candidates have been considered.
pitfalls: Return the sum itself, not its absolute difference from target.
Initialize the answer using an actual triplet rather than an arbitrary sentinel.
Maintain left < right so all three indices are distinct.
Move exactly one pointer according to whether the current sum is below or above target.
Sorting mutates nums unless a copy is sorted.
Duplicate-value skipping is not required because the goal is the closest sum, not a list of unique triplets.
knowledge.timeComplexity: O(n^2): sorting costs O(n log n), and the two-pointer scans across all fixed indices cost O(n^2).
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(log n) auxiliary space for a typical comparison sort; excluding sorting internals, the two-pointer procedure uses O(1) extra space.
knowledge.hint1: Consider sorting the values so that changing an index changes the sum predictably.
knowledge.hint2: After fixing one element, place one pointer immediately after it and another at the end of the array.
knowledge.hint3: Compare each triplet sum with the target: move the left pointer right when the sum is too small, and move the right pointer left when it is too large, updating the closest sum each time.

knowledge.summary: Count index tuples whose four values sum to zero by splitting the four arrays into two pairs. Store the frequency of every sum from nums1 and nums2, then count complementary sums from nums3 and nums4.
knowledge.pattern: Meet-in-the-middle with a hash map of pair-sum frequencies.
algorithm: Create a hash map cnt where cnt[s] is the number of index pairs (i, j) such that nums1[i] + nums2[j] = s.
Enumerate every pair of values c from nums3 and d from nums4.
For each pair sum t = c + d, add cnt[-t] to the answer because s + t must equal zero.
Return the accumulated answer.
pitfalls: Store frequencies rather than only recording whether a pair sum exists, because duplicate values and distinct index pairs must all be counted.
Look up the negated sum -(c + d), not c + d.
Do not deduplicate the arrays; tuples are defined by indices.
Avoid enumerating all four indices directly, which takes O(n^4) time.
In languages where numeric ranges are narrower, ensure pair sums and the accumulated count use a suitable integer type.
knowledge.timeComplexity: O(n^2): generating the first pair-sum frequencies takes O(n^2), and checking all pairs from the other two arrays takes O(n^2) expected time with a hash map.
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(n^2) in the worst case for the hash map of distinct pair sums.
knowledge.hint1: Try dividing the equation into two parts: nums1[i] + nums2[j] and nums3[k] + nums4[l].
knowledge.hint2: If one pair has sum s, the other pair must have sum -s. Consider precomputing information about all sums from one pair of arrays.
knowledge.hint3: Build a frequency map for every nums1[i] + nums2[j]. Then, for each nums3[k] + nums4[l], add the stored frequency of its negation.

knowledge.summary: Sort the array, fix the first two values, and find the remaining two values with a two-pointer scan. Sorting allows duplicate values to be skipped systematically so that every valid quadruplet is returned exactly once.
knowledge.pattern: Sorting + nested enumeration + two pointers, with duplicate elimination.
algorithm: Sort nums in nondecreasing order.
Enumerate the first index i from 0 through n - 4. If i > 0 and nums[i] equals nums[i - 1], skip it.
For each i, enumerate the second index j from i + 1 through n - 3. If j > i + 1 and nums[j] equals nums[j - 1], skip it.
Set left = j + 1 and right = n - 1.
While left < right, compute the sum of nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], and nums[right] using a sufficiently wide integer type.
If the sum is smaller than target, increment left. If it is larger than target, decrement right.
If the sum equals target, record the quadruplet, move both pointers inward, and skip repeated values at both pointer positions.
Return all recorded quadruplets.
pitfalls: Skipping duplicates at the wrong scope can remove valid results. For i, compare with i - 1 only when i > 0; for j, compare with j - 1 only when j > i + 1.
After finding a quadruplet, move both pointers and skip duplicate values on both sides.
The four-value sum can exceed a 32-bit signed integer even though each input value and target fit in that type. Use 64-bit arithmetic where necessary.
Maintain i < j < left < right so that all four selected indices are distinct.
Do not use a set as a substitute for correct duplicate handling when the sorted two-pointer method can avoid generating duplicates directly.
If adding min/max-sum pruning, compute bounds carefully with valid indices and wide arithmetic.
knowledge.timeComplexity: O(n^3): sorting costs O(n log n), while the two nested loops and linear two-pointer scan dominate.
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(log n) auxiliary space for a typical comparison sort, excluding the returned quadruplets; it may be O(1) if the language provides an in-place sort with constant auxiliary space.
knowledge.hint1: Sort the array first. How does ordering help both with uniqueness and with deciding which value to increase or decrease?
knowledge.hint2: Fix two indices i and j. The remaining task is a sorted 2Sum search in the suffix after j.
knowledge.hint3: Use left and right pointers for the final two values. After recording a match, move both inward and skip equal neighboring values; also skip repeated choices for i and j.

knowledge.summary: Treat each account as a node. Accounts belong to the same merged group when they are connected directly or transitively through shared emails. Use an email-to-account map to discover these connections, then collect and sort the unique emails for each connected component.
knowledge.pattern: Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) with hash maps. This is a connected-components problem where shared emails create edges between account indices.
algorithm: Create a Union-Find structure containing one node for each account index.
Maintain a map from each email to an account index where that email was previously seen.
For every email in every account, store the current account index if the email is new. If it was already seen, union the current account with the stored account.
Iterate over the accounts again. Find each account's representative and add all of its emails to a set associated with that representative.
For each representative, sort the component's unique emails and prepend the name from the representative account.
Return all constructed merged accounts in any order.
pitfalls: Do not merge accounts merely because their names are equal; only shared emails establish identity.
Connectivity is transitive: if account A shares an email with B and B shares another email with C, all three must be merged.
Use sets while collecting component emails so duplicate email occurrences do not appear in the result.
Call find before grouping accounts because an account's immediate parent may not be the final representative.
Sort only the emails in each merged account; the merged accounts themselves may be returned in any order.
Use path compression and union by size or rank to keep Union-Find operations efficient.
knowledge.timeComplexity: Let A be the number of accounts, E the total number of email occurrences, and U the number of unique emails. Union-Find processing takes O(E * alpha(A)) amortized. Collecting emails takes O(E), and sorting takes O(sum(k_i log k_i)) across components, bounded by O(U log U). Overall: O(E * alpha(A) + U log U).
knowledge.spaceComplexity: O(A + U) auxiliary space for the Union-Find arrays, email-to-account map, and grouped unique-email sets.
knowledge.hint1: Model each account index as a node. What piece of information can tell you that two nodes must belong to the same connected component?
knowledge.hint2: Keep a map from email to the first account index that contained it. When the same email appears again, connect the two account indices.
knowledge.hint3: Use Union-Find for the connections. After all unions, group emails by find(accountIndex), deduplicate them with sets, sort each group, and prepend the component's account name.
